items.question: Why can this creation not properly be called the first creation?
premises: In this creation all portions of dissolution and creation abide in the middle.
A first creation would not contain dissolution and creation as intermediate portions within it.
Therefore it is not fitting to call this creation the first.
items.inference: Because dissolution and creation are both present within it as middle phases, this creation cannot rightly be designated as the primordial first creation.
items.plain_english: In that creation, all the aspects of dissolution and creation exist in the middle; therefore it would not be fitting to call it the very first creation.

items.question: How can a first arising occur in a principle beyond place and time?
premises: The ultimate principle is beyond place and time.
A first arising presupposes temporal sequence.
This waking state is the primary state that partakes of unfolding.
items.inference: Since the principle transcends place and time, no literal first arising occurs there; rather, the waking state is the primary mode of unfolding.
items.plain_english: For in a principle beyond place and time, how could there be a first arising and so on? This waking state is the primary one, partaking of the state of unfolding.

items.question: From what highest form down to what lowest form do these powers unfold?
premises: Brahma is seated on the lotus of awakening of a portion of his own power.
The powers unfold beginning from the auspicious Śiva form.
They extend down to the form of Brahma.
items.inference: The powers of consciousness unfold in a graded descent from the supreme Śiva form to the Brahma form.
items.plain_english: This Brahma is seated on the lotus of awakening of a portion of his own power; these powers unfold beginning from the auspicious Śiva form and extending finally to the form of Brahma.

items.question: Can the Lord of consciousness be limited to a definite measurable extent?
premises: The powers of the Lord of consciousness unfold by assuming form.
One might try to say that the god is only this much.
Such a statement is considered as a possible attempt.
items.inference: Although the powers manifest in definite forms, the attempt to delimit the Lord to a fixed extent is only a provisional claim.
items.plain_english: The powers of the Lord of consciousness unfold by taking form. Even if one might try to say, 'This god is only so much,' such a claim is considered possible.

items.question: Why cannot the great Lord of consciousness be described as limited in extent?
premises: The great Lord's nature is consciousness.
Consciousness is immeasurable.
This point was stated clearly in the Prabodhapañcadaśikā.
items.inference: Because the great Lord is of the nature of immeasurable consciousness, he cannot truly be said to be limited.
items.plain_english: It cannot truly be said, because the great Lord, whose nature is consciousness, is immeasurable. I have stated this clearly in the Prabodhapañcadaśikā.

items.question: What distinguishes awareness from inert matter in terms of measurability?
premises: Limited manifestation is the characteristic of the inert.
Awareness is distinct from the inert.
Awareness is not measured.
items.inference: Because awareness cannot be measured, it is fundamentally different from inert matter, whose defining mark is limited manifestation.
items.plain_english: It has been said that limited manifestation is indeed the characteristic of the inert; awareness is distinct from the inert because it is not measured.

items.question: How does the immeasurable Lord appear as the measurable universe?
premises: The Lord is by nature free from measure.
He acts by the exercise of his own freedom.
By that freedom he makes himself into the moving and unmoving universe.
items.inference: Though immeasurable in essence, the Lord freely manifests himself as the measurable world of moving and unmoving beings.
items.plain_english: Even so, the god, who is himself beyond measure, by the exercise of his own freedom makes himself into the moving and unmoving universe.

items.question: Through what combinations of principles do the divisions of Śiva arise?
premises: The principles Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, and Aja are involved.
They function as arisen and about to arise.
They combine as singles, six, one, a triad, and three dyads.
items.inference: The manifold divisions of Śiva arise through specific combinatory arrangements of these principles in their arisen and emerging modes.
uncertainties: The precise mapping of each numerical grouping to specific Śiva divisions is compressed in this verse.
items.plain_english: Through Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, and Aja, in their arisen and about-to-arise forms, combining as single ones, as six, as one, as a triad, and as three dyads,

items.question: Why do the ten divisions of Śiva appear in manifold forms?
premises: The ten divisions of Śiva arise in a manifold state.
Consciousnesses are varied.
Their mixture produces further variation.
items.inference: The manifold condition of the ten Śiva divisions results from the mixture of varied forms of consciousness.
items.plain_english: There arises a manifold state of the ten divisions of Śiva; indeed, this is due to the mixture of varied consciousnesses.

items.question: How do differentiated knowledges arise even within what is called Śiva?
premises: Even in the state called Śiva, knowledges of difference appear.
These varied knowledges are extended or unfolded.
They arise when the left and right of the three faces come into union.
items.inference: Differentiated knowledges emerge within Śiva through the conjunction of the left and right aspects of the three faces.
items.plain_english: Even in what is called Śiva, varied knowledges of difference were unfolded when the left and right aspects of the three faces came together.

items.question: How does the Rudra division become eighteenfold?
premises: Each becomes a distinct power in relation to future, present, and arisen modes.
Six such powers are arranged in a triad.
This arrangement establishes the Rudra division eighteenfold.
items.inference: The Rudra division becomes eighteenfold through the triadic distribution of six powers across future, present, and arisen modes.
items.plain_english: Then, as each becomes a distinct power through the future, present, and arisen modes, the six in a triad make the Rudra division established in eighteen forms.

items.question: Why do the divisions of Śiva become innumerable?
premises: Each unit is declared to be five-faced.
The system is already divided into ten and eighteen.
Further subdivision by faces multiplies the divisions.
items.inference: Because each division is itself five-faced, the ten-and-eighteenfold scheme expands into innumerable divisions.
items.plain_english: Since each is declared to be five-faced, what is divided into ten and eighteen becomes innumerable through further divisions.

items.question: Why is the detailed enumeration of divisions not mere repetition?
premises: The divisions are variegated by each one's own knowledge and action as previously described.
These distinctions are determined within those divisions.
Distinct knowledge and action prevent sameness.
items.inference: Because each division is distinguished by its own knowledge and action, the account is not repetitive.
items.plain_english: Because in them the distinctions are determined by each one's own knowledge and action as stated before, there is no mere repetition.

items.question: How can diverse practices and actions all lead to the abode of Śiva?
premises: Awareness, practice, and the sequence of action differ in each case.
These differences are declared in their respective contexts.
Yet all of them go to the abode of Śiva.
items.inference: Although knowledge and practice vary by context, all valid forms ultimately converge in the abode of Śiva.
items.plain_english: For awareness, practice, and the sequence of action are indeed different in each case, as declared there; yet all of them lead to the abode of Śiva.

items.question: What analogy explains how all knowledges and actions converge in the great Lord?
premises: All drops of water come to rest in the great ocean.
All knowledges and actions are diverse in form.
The great Lord is the ocean of consciousness.
items.inference: Just as all water drops rest in the ocean, all knowledges and actions ultimately rest in the great Lord, the ocean of consciousness.
items.plain_english: Just as all drops of water come to rest in the great ocean, so all knowledges and actions come to rest in the great Lord, the ocean of consciousness.

items.question: How do all forms of knowledge and action ultimately return to Śiva?
premises: Even limited water on earth is drawn up by the sun and returns to the great ocean through rain.
All knowledge and action in the world arise in various ways.
Some arise by themselves and some through transmission by others.
items.inference: By analogy with the water cycle, all knowledge and action, whether direct or transmitted, ultimately merge in the ocean of Śiva.
items.plain_english: Even limited water on earth is drawn up by the sun's rays and returns again to the great ocean through rain; so too, all knowledge and action in the world, some arising by themselves and some through others in succession, sink into the ocean of Śiva.

items.question: What is the nature of the supreme heart-mark described at the right end?
premises: At the right end there is a heart-mark regarded as supreme.
That mark is identified with the heart.
It contains within itself all created beings in fullness.
items.inference: The supreme heart-mark is not empty but inwardly contains the fullness of all created beings.
items.plain_english: And that heart-mark at the right end, regarded as the supreme heart, is also fully filled with all created beings taken within it.

items.question: Why is that supreme heart-mark described as dark and bearing the form of darkness?
premises: It devours the rays of māyā that produce difference.
By doing so it functions as the dissolver of all.
Dissolution of all differentiated light is represented as darkness.
items.inference: Because it absorbs all differentiating māyā and dissolves all, the supreme heart-mark appears dark, bearing the form of darkness.
items.plain_english: And because it devours the rays of māyā that produce difference, that, as the dissolver of all, is dark and bears the form of darkness.

items.question: What scriptural teaching supports the identification of the Lord's darkness with dissolution?
premises: The Vijñānaśāstra contains a teaching by the great Lord.
That teaching states that all space is dissolved in the head.
This supports the description of the Lord's darkness.
items.inference: The scriptural statement that all space dissolves in the head confirms the Lord's darkness as the state of universal dissolution.
items.plain_english: Therefore it is stated in the Vijñānaśāstra by the great Lord: 'All space is dissolved in the head,' and so forth, referring to the darkness of the Lord.

items.question: When and how should the Bhairava form of darkness be contemplated?
premises: The Bhairava form is associated with darkness and dissolution.
A dark night at the arrival of the dark fortnight corresponds to that form.
Contemplators should meditate on that hard-to-name form for a long time.
items.inference: The Bhairava form of darkness should be contemplated for a long time on a dark night at the coming of the dark fortnight.
items.plain_english: Thus, on a dark night at the arrival of the dark fortnight, one should contemplate for a long time the Bhairava form, which is hard to name, by those who practice contemplation.

items.question: What characterizes the nondual state where ignorance and karma do not bind?
premises: In that state light, suffering, and darkness are covered by nonduality.
There is no connection with ignorance and karma.
Dependence and similar limiting conditions are not seen there.
items.inference: The nondual state transcends the oppositions of light, suffering, and darkness, and therefore excludes bondage by ignorance, karma, and dependence.
uncertainties: The exact syntactic relation of svar duḥkhaṃ tamo in the source line is compact; the sense follows the nondual covering indicated by advayasaṃvṛte.
items.plain_english: And it is said: where light, suffering, and darkness are covered by nonduality, there is no connection with ignorance and karma, because dependence and the like are not seen.

items.question: How do the four faces appear within the dark Bhairava body?
premises: The Bhairava body is of the form of darkness.
The four faces are present within it.
They shine by being inwardly dissolved.
items.inference: Within the dark Bhairava body, the four faces shine in a latent, inwardly dissolved manner.
items.plain_english: Therefore, in this Bhairava body of the form of darkness, the group of four faces shines fully by being inwardly dissolved.

items.question: How does the fourfold structure become sixteenfold in the Bhairava body?
premises: Each aspect can be about to emerge, emerged, about to withdraw, or withdrawn.
These states apply simultaneously.
The division yields a sixteenfold structure.
items.inference: By the simultaneous application of emergence and withdrawal states, the structure becomes sixteenfold.
items.plain_english: As about to emerge, emerged, about to withdraw, and withdrawn, this division therefore becomes simultaneously sixteenfold.

items.question: How does the Bhairava scripture become an eight-times-eight system within Śiva?
premises: The teaching enters the right, emissive, heart, and autonomous aspects in Śiva.
The sixteenfold structure is further articulated.
The scripture named Bhairava becomes eight-times-eight simultaneously.
items.inference: By entering the autonomous Śiva through its right, emissive, and heart aspects, the Bhairava scripture unfolds simultaneously as an eight-times-eight system.
uncertainties: The technical mapping of dakṣa, vaisargika, hārda, and svatantra to the full eight-times-eight structure is compressed in this verse.
items.plain_english: Entering the right, emissive, heart, and autonomous aspects in Śiva, the scripture named Bhairava becomes simultaneously an eight-times-eight system.
